El País English, 17 Nov 2026 17:35 GMT

The founder of the world’s largest chipmaker makes his first public comments since stepping down last week amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy

In his first public comments since his abrupt departure from Nvidia, Jensen Huang said on Tuesday that he would be willing to return as chief executive of the technology giant. The man who, until a few days ago, led the world’s largest chipmaker stepped down amid a scandal involving his extramarital relationships, one of them with an executive at a Singapore-based company whom U.S. intelligence officials believe was a Chinese spy.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a statement posted on X. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of the shareholders, the employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an…

Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into Huang on November 8 after he admitted in a letter to having had an affair with Alice Huang, the founder of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that purchased about $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips. A report by The New York Times stated that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang was an operative for Beijing who diverted Nvidia chips to China. The Chinese government has denied that Alice Huang was working as a spy for China.

Days later, Jensen Huang’s departure from the semiconductor giant was announced, and he was replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer Colette Kress.

In his statement, Huang acknowledged that he had failed to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia” and had made “serious mistakes in [his] personal life.” “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. [...] I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he added.

U.S. authorities also confirmed that they are continuing an investigation into Megaspeed that began in 2024. Amid tensions the matter has generated within the Trump administration, the Departments of Justice and Commerce said they are jointly investigating whether the Singapore-based company engaged in criminal conduct in its dealings with Nvidia.

The inquiry began at the Department of Commerce and was later transferred to the Department of Justice after Trump returned to office. “After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations,” the statement said.

“In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its ‘no sell’ list,” the statement continued.

Officials from the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, together with Singaporean authorities, then conducted an on-site inspection of Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang. “Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed,” the statement said.

The New York Times had previously reported that the investigation into Nvidia’s sales to Megaspeed was abruptly paused last year after one of Nvidia’s legal advisers requested details of the inquiry from Commerce Department officials.

Some of the outstanding questions may be clarified when Jensen Huang and Nvidia’s chief legal officer, Tim Teter, appear before Congress on December 1 and December 2, respectively. They are scheduled to be interviewed by members of several House of Representatives committees, including the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Representative Brian Mast, the Republican chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement on Tuesday. “The ​American people need answers on Mr. Huang and ​Nvidia’s role in ⁠allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal."

Since Huang’s departure, the chorus of voices calling for his return has grown louder. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang returned to lead Nvidia, while Elon Musk, chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla, and Silicon Valley entrepreneurs such as Amjad Masad of Replit and Tim Sweeney of Epic Games have backed calls for his reinstatement.

Musk, for his part, argued that Nvidia without Huang could jeopardize future sales deals at a company that is central to the artificial intelligence race. He suggested that many of Nvidia’s agreements ultimately came down to “a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract.” “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost,” he wrote on X.

Meanwhile, amid a scandal that has weighed on Nvidia’s stock price, investors remain concerned about whether the company can maintain its dominance in chipmaking and retain the confidence of cloud-service providers and AI laboratories.

Also on Tuesday, Nvidia announced the creation of a committee made up of board members and independent experts to oversee compliance with global trade regulations and Washington’s national security policies.

“We are committed to working constructively with [U.S.] government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation, ”said Harvey Jones, chairman of NVIDIA’s Board of Directors, in a statement.
